<article class="publication">
  <div class="publication-year" data-i18n="st.forthcoming">Forthcoming</div>
  <div>
    <h3>Living Standards in Ghana, 1955–2005</h3>
    <p>I. Martins</p>
    <p class="journal"><em>Labour and Work in Ghana Since Independence</em> · <span data-i18n="st.editedby">Edited by</span> Gareth Austin, Akua Britwum, Lamine Doumbia, Andreas Eckert<span data-i18n="w.oxand">, and</span> Nana Yaw Sapong. London: Bloomsbury Academic</p>
    <p class="finding" data-i18n="find.ghana">Using consumption baskets matched to the diets of Ghana’s three ecological zones, I show that national baskets understate living standards in the northern savannah, and that the widening gap between regions in 1988–2005 came mainly from rural areas.</p>

    <details class="abstract"><summary data-i18n="st.abstract">Abstract</summary><div class="abstract-text" lang="en"><p>This paper constructs regional welfare ratios for Ghana from 1955 to 2005, combining five rounds of the Ghana Living Standards Survey with archival wage and price data. Using Allen-type consumption baskets calibrated to the dietary patterns of Ghana’s three ecological zones, I show that national baskets systematically misrepresent regional living standards in countries with significant dietary heterogeneity. Under a national basket priced at regional levels, several northern regions appear unable to meet subsistence. When the basket composition is allowed to reflect zone-specific diets, welfare ratios improve substantially in the savannah regions, where local staples (millet, sorghum) are cheaper than the cassava and plantain that dominate the national basket. I further decompose regional welfare by urban and rural status, showing that both urban and rural areas are diverging across regions, but that rural divergence is far more severe. The aggregate widening of regional inequality in Ghana over 1988–2005 is driven primarily by the rural sector.</p></div></details>
  </div>
</article>

    <h3>Från arbetskraft till kapital: Slaveriets ekonomiska logik i globalt perspektiv</h3>
    <p>I. Martins <span data-i18n="w.and">and</span> E. Green</p>
    <p class="journal"><em>Statsvetenskaplig tidskrift</em></p>

<article class="publication">
  <div class="publication-year">2026</div>
  <div>
    <h3><a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/ereh/heag012">Capital and Coercion: Slavery after the 1807 Import Ban in the Cape Colony</a></h3>
    <p>I. Martins</p>
    <p class="journal"><em>European Review of Economic History</em> · heag012</p>
    <p class="finding" data-i18n="find.capcoer">After Britain banned slave imports in 1807, wealthier households in Stellenbosch and Graaff-Reinet kept accumulating enslaved people, holding them as capital assets in a colony where capital was scarce.</p>

    <a class="paper-link" href="https://www.icpsr.umich.edu/sites/icpsr/view/studies/237703"><span data-i18n="st.replication">Replication package</span> ↗</a>
    <details class="abstract"><summary data-i18n="st.abstract">Abstract</summary><div class="abstract-text" lang="en"><p>The 1807 Slave Trade Act banned slave imports across the British Empire, triggering a sharp supply shock. Using newly digitised tax censuses from the Cape Colony, this article examines slave accumulation patterns in Stellenbosch and Graaff-Reinet following the supply shock. Despite stark ecological and institutional differences, both districts show similar post-abolition trajectories. This challenges models linking coercion to land–labour ratios, supervision costs, or frontier openness. Testing five frameworks, the paper finds the strongest support for the view of slaves as capital assets. Wealthier households continued accumulating slaves, suggesting slavery persisted not only as labour but as an asset strategy amid capital scarcity.</p></div></details>
  </div>
</article>
<article class="publication">
  <div class="publication-year">2026</div>
  <div>
    <h3><a href="https://doi.org/10.1017/S1740022825100296">Theoretical Foundations of the Economics of Slavery: Enslaved People as Capital Investments in the Atlantic World</a></h3>
    <p>I. Martins <span data-i18n="w.and">and</span> E. Green</p>
    <p class="journal"><em>Journal of Global History</em> · 21(1), 22–40</p>
    <p class="finding" data-i18n="find.theory">Comparing the United States, Brazil and the Cape Colony, we show that enslavers held enslaved people as both labour and capital investment, and that this investment role is key to explaining why slavery persisted.</p>

    <details class="abstract"><summary data-i18n="st.abstract">Abstract</summary><div class="abstract-text" lang="en"><p>Despite the prevalence of slavery in world history, our understanding of its persistence remains limited. Most previous studies focus primarily on slavery as a labour contract, indistinguishable from other coercive arrangements such as serfdom. More recent literature on slavery in the United States shows that enslaved people also played an important role as financial instruments. In this article, we extend the investigation by comparing slavery in the United States with that in Brazil and the Cape Colony. We show that despite significant geographic, demographic, and economic differences, slavery was not merely a labour arrangement in the three cases but a unique institution that gave enslavers complete rights over mobile property. Slavery provided access to both labour and capital, with the capital investment dimension being key to understanding its persistence. We argue that understanding slavery’s persistence requires recognizing enslaved people as both sources of labour and capital investment.</p></div></details>
  </div>
</article>

    <h3><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.eeh.2024.101620">Fertility responses to short-term economic stress: Price volatility and wealth shocks in a pre-transitional settler colony</a></h3>
    <p>J. Cilliers, M. Mariotti<span data-i18n="w.oxand">, and</span> I. Martins</p>
    <p class="journal"><em>Explorations in Economic History</em> · 101620</p>
    <p class="finding" data-i18n="find.fertility">Cape settler households that lost slave wealth at emancipation in 1834 appear to have postponed births, while price volatility had no clear effect on conceptions.</p>

    <a class="paper-link" href="https://www.icpsr.umich.edu/sites/icpsr/view/studies/208362"><span data-i18n="st.replication">Replication package</span> ↗</a>
    <details class="abstract"><summary data-i18n="st.abstract">Abstract</summary><div class="abstract-text" lang="en"><p>This paper examines the effects of short-term economic stress, captured by general price volatility and a negative wealth shock on short-run fertility behavior in the rural pre-transitional society of the Cape Colony. First, we link complete birth histories of settler women from the South African Families database to consumer price index data to examine the effect of price volatility on conceptions. Next, we link the same birth histories to slave owner and slave emancipation data to examine the effect of a negative wealth shock on conception. Upon slave emancipation in 1834, former slave owners received on average only between 40 and 50 % of the market value of their slaves as compensation, resulting in a substantial reduction in their wealth. Relying on event history models that look simultaneously at stopping and spacing, we do not find strong evidence in support of fertility control in response to general price volatility. We do find greater variance in birth interval lengths for former slaveholding households during and immediately after emancipation, suggesting that a negative wealth shock is associated with increased fertility limitation through postponement in this context.</p></div></details>
  </div>
</article>
<article class="publication">

  <div>
    <h3><a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s12116-023-09392-1">Resilience to shrinking as a catch-up strategy: a comparison of Brazil and Indonesia, 1964–2019</a></h3>
    <p>T. Axelsson <span data-i18n="w.and">and</span> I. Martins</p>
    <p class="journal"><em>Studies in Comparative International Development</em> · 59(3), 491–516</p>
    <p class="finding" data-i18n="find.brazil">We argue that differences in structural transformation, autonomy and inclusion explain why Indonesia has weathered economic shrinking better than Brazil since 1964.</p>

    <details class="abstract"><summary data-i18n="st.abstract">Abstract</summary><div class="abstract-text" lang="en"><p>Development economics has long focused on growth patterns to explain countries’ ability to catch up and forge ahead. We argue, however, that resilience to economic shrinking matters more. Using the examples of Brazil and Indonesia, we propose that a framework consisting of social capabilities—namely structural transformation, autonomy, and inclusion—can explain why Indonesia is more resilient to economic shrinking than Brazil and why the country is more likely to be successful in its catching-up process.</p></div></details>
  </div>
</article>
<article class="publication">
  <div class="publication-year">2024</div>
  <div>
    <h3><a href="https://doi.org/10.1108/IJDI-06-2023-0168">Inequality, poverty, and resilience to economic shrinking</a></h3>
    <p>A. Smythe, I. Martins<span data-i18n="w.oxand">, and</span> M. Andersson</p>
    <p class="journal"><em>International Journal of Development Issues</em> · 23(1), 40–81</p>
    <p class="finding" data-i18n="find.poverty">Across 23 developing countries over 42 years, falling poverty is associated with fewer episodes of economic shrinking, while changes in income inequality show no such relationship.</p>

    <details class="abstract"><summary data-i18n="st.abstract">Abstract</summary><div class="abstract-text" lang="en"><p><strong>Purpose.</strong> With the recognition that generating economic growth is not the same as sustaining it, the challenge to catch-up and growth literature is discerning between these processes. Recent research suggests that the decline in the frequency of “shrinking” episodes is more important for long-term development than higher growth rates. By using a framework centred around social capabilities, this study aims to investigate the effects of income inequality and poverty on economic shrinking frequency, as opposed to previous literature that has exclusively had a growth focus. The aim is to investigate how and why some societies might be more resilient to economic shrinking.</p><p><strong>Design/methodology/approach.</strong> The research is a quantitative study, and the authors build a longitudinal data set including 23 developing countries throughout 42 years to test the paper’s purpose. This study uses country and period fixed-effects specifications as well as cross-sectional graphical representations to investigate the relationship between proxies of economic inclusivity and the frequency of shrinking episodes.</p><p><strong>Findings.</strong> The authors demonstrate that while inclusive societies are more resilient to shrinking overall, it is changes in poverty levels, but not changes in income inequality, that appear to be correlated with economic shrinking frequency. Inequality, while still an important element to explain countries’ growth potential as an initial condition, does not seem to make the sample more resilient to shrinking. The authors conclude that the mechanisms in which poverty and inequality are correlated with the catch-up process must run through different channels. Ultimately, processes that explain growth may intersect but not always overlap with the ones that explain resilience to shrinking.</p><p><strong>Originality/value.</strong> The need for inclusive growth in long-term development has been championed for decades, yet inclusion has seldom been explored from the shrinking perspective. Though poverty reduction is already an important mainstream political objective, this paper differentiates itself by providing an alternate viewpoint of why this is important. Income inequality could have more of an economic growth limiting effect, while poverty reduction could be required to build resilience to economic shrinking. Developing countries will need both growth and resilience to shrinking, to catch-up with higher-income economies, which policymakers might need to balance carefully.</p></div></details>
  </div>
</article>

  <div>
    <h3><a href="https://doi.org/10.58875/WBCQ3772">An age of disentangled research?</a></h3>
    <p>I. Martins <span data-i18n="w.and">and</span> S. Schwaag Serger</p>
    <p class="journal"><em>Issues in Science and Technology</em> · 40(1), 38–43</p>
    <p class="finding" data-i18n="find.disentangled">Coauthorship between Chinese and US researchers has begun to decline, and we ask what growing political constraints mean for international science.</p>

    <details class="abstract"><summary data-i18n="st.abstract">Abstract</summary><div class="abstract-text" lang="en"><p>This article examines the emerging decline in international research collaboration, especially between China and the United States, and asks whether we are entering a new era of globally fragmented science. While US–China coauthorship is decreasing, European trends are more uneven. Drawing on bibliometric data and institutional analysis, the authors argue that growing political constraints and institutional caution are shifting global scientific cooperation into a more divided, uncertain phase, raising urgent questions about the future of science as a public good.</p></div></details>
  </div>
</article>

    <h3><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.eeh.2022.101506">Legacies of loss: The health outcomes of slaveholder compensation in the British Cape Colony</a></h3>
    <p>I. Martins, J. Cilliers<span data-i18n="w.oxand">, and</span> J. Fourie</p>
    <p class="journal"><em>Explorations in Economic History</em> · 101506</p>
    <p class="finding" data-i18n="find.legacies">Slaveholders who lost more wealth through the partial compensation of 1834 lived slightly shorter lives, an effect concentrated among older owners; their children and grandchildren were unaffected.</p>

    <a class="paper-link" href="https://www.icpsr.umich.edu/sites/icpsr/view/studies/183526"><span data-i18n="st.replication">Replication package</span> ↗</a>
    <details class="abstract"><summary data-i18n="st.abstract">Abstract</summary><div class="abstract-text" lang="en"><p>Can wealth shocks have intergenerational health consequences? We use the partial compensation slaveholders received after the 1834 slave emancipation in the British Cape Colony to measure the intergenerational effects of a wealth loss on longevity. We find that a greater loss of slave wealth shortened the lifespans of the generation of slaveholders that experienced the shock albeit these effects are usually small and mostly confined to older cohorts of slaveholders who likely exploited slaves both as labor and capital inputs. The lifespans of those of the second generation who survived infancy were unaffected by the shortfalls and no effects of the shortfall were found for the third generation.</p></div></details>
  </div>
</article>

<article class="publication">

  <div>
    <h3>The Case for Artisanal Doctoral Supervision</h3>
    <p>I. Martins</p>
    <p class="journal"><em>Studies in Higher Education</em> · <span data-i18n="st.rr">Revise and resubmit</span></p>

    <p class="finding" data-i18n="find.artisanal">Universities track doctoral students through study plans and progress reviews. I propose revisable plans and brief records of reasons, so that supervisors remain accountable and students can still change course when new evidence calls for it.</p>
    <details class="abstract"><summary data-i18n="st.abstract">Abstract</summary><div class="abstract-text" lang="en"><p>Universities increasingly organise doctoral supervision through study plans and progress reviews. These instruments protect students by making promised support verifiable. They also establish an early account of the research against which later progress is judged. In humanities research, new evidence may unsettle that account, and a change that improves the thesis can then look like a failure to keep to the plan. This conceptual article brings together research on doctoral supervision and research on how universities assess academic work to develop a typology of supervision. It distinguishes structure, which makes support reliable, from judgement, which helps students decide what a discovery means for their thesis. Their combination produces nominal, unstructured, bureaucratic, and artisanal supervision. Bureaucratic supervision combines reliable support with weak judgement and suits reviews that measure progress against the plan. Artisanal supervision uses reliable structure to make room for justified changes to the thesis within the time a doctorate allows. The article argues that formal records capture intellectual judgement poorly and can steer supervision towards what they record. It proposes revisable plans and brief, protected records of reasons, so that universities can hold supervision to account while leaving room for discovery.</p></div></details>
  </div>
</article>
<article class="publication">

  <div>
    <h3>Retrieval-Restricted Reasoning: Supporting Scholarly Synthesis with Language Models</h3>
    <p>I. Martins</p>
    <p class="journal"><em>Historical Methods: A Journal of Quantitative and Interdisciplinary History</em> · <span data-i18n="st.rr">Revise and resubmit</span></p>
    <p class="finding" data-i18n="find.rrr">I built a method that lets language models write literature reviews only from sources the researcher supplies; across 100 test reviews with 4,767 citations, 99 contained none of the five measured citation errors.</p>

    <a class="paper-link" href="https://www.icpsr.umich.edu/sites/icpsr/view/studies/246321"><span data-i18n="st.replication">Replication package</span> ↗</a>
    <details class="abstract"><summary data-i18n="st.abstract">Abstract</summary><div class="abstract-text" lang="en"><p>Large language models can synthesize scholarship quickly, while the relation between their prose and the underlying sources often remains difficult to verify. This paper introduces Retrieval-Restricted Reasoning (RRR), an architecture for model-assisted synthesis over a researcher-defined corpus. RRR admits page-level evidence, binds it to stable identifiers before composition, renders citations from those records, and records a refusal when the collection cannot sustain the question. I evaluate the architecture through repeated runs on a contested economic-history literature. Across 100 full-RRR runs, the reviews contained 4,767 parsed citations. Ninety-nine reviews were free of the five measured error classes. One review contained a single citation identity that did not resolve to the declared collection; the audit found no invalid page, citation-format, or quotation error. A corpus-only instruction reduced boundary crossing substantially, and page-based comparison conditions showed that traceability arose through a layered contract of retrieval, evidence binding, rendering, writer intervention, and final checking. Model and workflow comparisons further separated writing capability from the preservation of a checkable source path. RRR supports historical synthesis by keeping claims connected to inspectable scholarship while leaving the researcher to judge the corpus and the historical interpretations built from it.</p></div></details>
  </div>
</article>

  <div>
    <h3>Slave Emancipation and Farm Output in the Cape Colony</h3>
    <p>I. Martins</p>
    <p class="journal"><em>Cliometrica</em> · <span data-i18n="st.submitted">Submitted</span></p>
    <p class="finding" data-i18n="find.emancipation">Large mixed farms in Stellenbosch that lost more uncompensated slave wealth at emancipation produced markedly less wine and grain afterwards, consistent with the loss of enslaved people as collateral for credit.</p>

    <a class="paper-link" href="https://www.icpsr.umich.edu/sites/icpsr/view/studies/248667"><span data-i18n="st.replication">Replication package</span> ↗</a>
    <details class="abstract"><summary data-i18n="st.abstract">Abstract</summary><div class="abstract-text" lang="en"><p>Slave emancipation reorganised labour and removed a legally protected form of wealth that had supported collateralised credit. Using a household-level panel of farmers in Stellenbosch, Cape Colony (1824–1844), this study links annual tax censuses to slave valuation and compensation records to measure uncompensated slave wealth after the Slavery Abolition Act. The compensation scheme created a farm-level gap between locally assessed slave values and cash awards, providing a measure of balance-sheet exposure to abolition. Farmer and year fixed effects compare the same farms over time after conditioning on labour availability, household size, and livestock. Output losses were concentrated among large mixed producers, the farmers most likely to have combined enslaved labour with slave-backed credit. Among these farms, an interquartile-range increase in uncompensated value per enslaved person is associated with losses equal to 20 percent of pre-emancipation wine output and 31 percent of pre-emancipation grain output after full emancipation. The findings show that emancipation’s productive consequences reflected labour reorganisation and the destruction of a property right that had supported credit and agricultural production.</p></div></details>
  </div>
</article>
<article class="publication">

  <div>
    <h3>Democracy and Rural Inequality in Kenya, 1997–2010</h3>
    <p>J. Makuei <span data-i18n="w.and">and</span> I. Martins</p>
    <p class="journal"><em>African Affairs</em> · <span data-i18n="st.submitted">Submitted</span></p>

    <p class="finding" data-i18n="find.kenya">Across 31 Kenyan constituencies from 1997 to 2010, rural households gained better access to fertiliser, roads and markets after the first democratic transfer of power, while the gap in household wealth between constituencies barely changed.</p>
    <details class="abstract"><summary data-i18n="st.abstract">Abstract</summary><div class="abstract-text" lang="en"><p>Democratic transitions can expand access to rural infrastructure and productive inputs. It remains unclear whether they can reduce entrenched inequalities in household wealth. We examine this issue in the context of Kenya’s first inter-party transfer of presidential power. We combine electoral outcomes in 31 constituencies with five rounds of rural household surveys from 1997 to 2010. Fertiliser use and road and market access improved over time. In contrast, the spatial distribution of household assets was far more stable: constituencies that were initially advantaged stayed so. Moreover, we find no subsequent economic or public programme benefits for constituencies that elected Mwai Kibaki as president in 2007. Kenya illustrates a key challenge facing Africa’s new democracies. While access can improve over a decade, entrenched inequality can persist.</p></div></details>
  </div>
</article>

  <div>
    <h3>Held by the Elite: Monopoly Rights and Family Fortunes at the Cape of Good Hope, 1680–1794</h3>
    <p>I. Martins, J. Schoots<span data-i18n="w.oxand">, and</span> E. Green</p>


    <p class="finding" data-i18n="find.pachten">The Dutch East India Company auctioned the right to sell alcohol at the Cape every year. The settlers who won these rights already owned enslaved people more often than others, and those who ran them as a business accumulated more, while their families lasted no longer than other settler families.</p>
    <details class="abstract"><summary data-i18n="st.abstract">Abstract</summary><div class="abstract-text" lang="en"><p>Many accounts of early modern elites hold that the privileges states sold made their holders rich and their families lasting. We test this for the alcohol retail rights (\textit{pachten}) that the Dutch East India Company auctioned each year at the Cape of Good Hope, 1680–1794, following every holder through auction records, an annual household census and a genealogical register, against settlers who never held a \textit{pacht}. A core of established operators kept their lots, paying at least as much as outsiders. Future holders already owned enslaved people more often than other settlers, and Cape-born ones had married into \textit{pachter} families three and a half times as often as other Cape-born men. Operators who held intensively from the start accumulated enslaved people, and one-year holders show no measurable change. \textit{Pachter} families lasted no longer than comparable settler families and married among themselves no more often. Sold every year at open auction, the privilege consolidated the position of slaveholding households and rewarded those who ran it as a business, without founding a lasting elite.</p></div></details>
  </div>
</article>
<article class="publication">

  <div>
    <h3>Catch-up and Resilience to Shrinking, 1890–2019</h3>
    <p>A. Smythe <span data-i18n="w.and">and</span> I. Martins</p>


    <p class="finding" data-i18n="find.catchup">Across 105 countries since 1955, productivity and inputs often moved in opposite directions, and a country’s earlier record of growing and shrinking helps predict its later expansion.</p>
    <details class="abstract"><summary data-i18n="st.abstract">Abstract</summary><div class="abstract-text" lang="en"><p>Growth depends on both gains in expansion and losses in contraction. We present a production-focused account of long-term economic growth and shrinking. We disaggregate shifts in the production function from movements along the production function, to provide a reconciliation of traditional growth accounting and the growing-and-shrinking framework. This synthesis exposes production patterns hidden behind overall growth. We find shifts in productivity and changes in input levels frequently move in opposite directions for a sample of 105 countries over the period 1955–2019. To illustrate the role of outside factors, we contrast production responses to an increase versus decrease in the global prices of a country’s exports. A decline in prices is followed by a backward movement along the production function, primarily through a lasting fall in capital services per capita. We examine whether decadal production histories contain clues for future catch-up. Patterns in 10-year production histories that originated between 1964 and 1989 select countries with significantly greater expansionary gains in the 1990s and 2000s. The earlier record of growing and shrinking also improves predictions of later expansion beyond the information contained in standard growth accounting.</p></div></details>
  </div>
</article>
